l: thoughts, The Great Learning
s: Thoughts are made sincere by allowing no self-deception and by being watchful over oneself when alone. Sincere thoughts lead to a rectified heart.

l: the Son of Heaven, The Great Learning
s: The Son of Heaven, like all people, must consider cultivation of the person the root of everything besides.

l: the sovereign, The Great Learning
s: The sovereign makes the people filial, brotherly, and compassionate by treating the aged, elders, and young and helpless properly. The sovereign gains the kingdom through the people and virtue, but loses it through a want of goodness.

l: the superior man, The Great Learning
s: The superior man uses his utmost endeavors, knows where to rest, and cultivates himself through learning and self-culture. He is watchful over himself when alone and makes his thoughts sincere.

l: the Book of Poetry, The Great Learning
s: The Book of Poetry is cited to teach resting, self-culture, reverence, remembrance of former kings, family order, and the proper conduct of rulers. Its passages also describe rulers as parents of the people and warn that the great decree is not easily preserved.

l: wealth, The Great Learning
s: Wealth is the result, while virtue is the root. Accumulating wealth scatters the people, whereas allowing wealth to be scattered among them collects the people; wealth should not be treated as the state's true prosperity.

l: the cultivation of the person, The Great Learning
s: The cultivation of the person depends on rectifying the heart and is the root of everything besides. It enables the regulation of the family and the proper government of the state.

l: the regulation of the family, The Great Learning
s: The regulation of the family depends on cultivation of the person and allows the ruler to teach the state through filial piety, fraternal submission, and kindness. A rightly ordered household provides an example for the people.

l: the government of the state, The Great Learning
s: The government of the state depends on the regulation of the family and on the ruler's own conduct. It makes the whole kingdom peaceful and happy when the ruler possesses good qualities and treats the people properly.

l: filial piety, The Great Learning
s: Filial piety is a quality through which the sovereign should be served. When the sovereign behaves properly toward the aged, the people become filial.

l: fraternal submission, The Great Learning
s: Fraternal submission is a quality through which elders and superiors should be served. When the sovereign behaves properly toward elders, the people learn brotherly submission.

l: benevolence, The Great Learning
s: Benevolence leads rulers such as Yao and Shun to be followed by the people. A sovereign who loves benevolence is associated with people who love righteousness.

l: the ruler’s virtue, The Great Learning
s: The ruler’s virtue is the root of the people, territory, wealth, and resources for expenditure. A virtuous ruler uses wealth to make himself more distinguished, while a vicious ruler accumulates wealth at the expense of his life.

l: the people’s righteousness, The Great Learning
s: The people’s righteousness supports the completion of the sovereign's affairs. A state's prosperity is found in righteousness rather than in wealth or pecuniary gain.

l: a minister, The Great Learning
s: A minister should be plain, sincere, upright, generous, able to bear and employ capable people, and free from jealousy. A minister who seeks imposts from the people is worse than one who robs the house of its revenues, and a jealous minister endangers the state.

l: the measuring-square principle, The Great Learning
s: The measuring-square principle requires a person not to impose on inferiors or superiors what he dislikes receiving himself. It is the principle by which the ruler regulates his conduct.

l: The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The Doctrine of the Mean presents a teaching on the Path of duty: Heaven gives humanity its Nature, and living in accord with it requires unceasing self-watchfulness. Its central ideal is the Mean, expressed through Equilibrium before feelings arise and Harmony when they act in due degree; their perfection brings order and flourishing to heaven and earth. Chung-ni and the Master contrast the superior man, who holds to the Mean with caution, sincerity, humility, and perseverance, with the mean man, who lacks caution and seeks notoriety. The Master laments that perfect virtue and the path of the Mean are rare, difficult to understand, easily exceeded or missed, and hard to sustain. Shun and Hui exemplify wise, firm adherence to it, while Tsze-lu’s question leads to an account of strong yet gentle and unchanging energy. The work then brings the Way into ordinary life: reciprocity, careful speech, self-rectification, acceptance of Heaven’s appointments, proper conduct in every station, and harmonious family relations. It portrays spiritual beings as subtly present in sacrifice, and presents filial piety, especially through Shun, King Wan, King Chi, King Wu, and the duke of Chau, as carrying forward forefathers’ purposes through rule, ceremony, mourning, and ancestral offerings. Government depends on proper persons, rulerly character, universal duties and virtues, preparation, and sincerity. Sincerity and intelligence entail one another; complete sincerity develops one’s own nature and those of other people, animals, and things, assists Heaven and Earth, transforms others, foreknows omens, and becomes ceaseless, vast, and Heaven-like. The Sage and ideal ruler preserve ceremony, study and practice the Mean, establish standards only with proper virtue and sovereignty, and become enduring models for the kingdom. The final chapters elevate Chung-ni, the sage ruler, and the wholly sincere person as Heaven-like figures, before returning to the superior man’s hidden virtue: sincere self-cultivation without display can move people toward virtue and happy tranquility.

l: The Doctrine of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: translated_by James Legge The Doctrine of the Mean explains the Nature, the Path of duty, the superior man, Equilibrium, and Harmony.

l: Heaven, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Heaven is a vast, enduring source of Nature, sincerity, appointments, nourishment, and transforming operations. It confers what is called the Nature and makes appointments that the superior man quietly awaits without murmuring. It is bountiful to beings according to their qualities: nourishing what flourishes, overthrowing what is ready to fall, and granting dignity and the throne as favors. Large, substantial, high, brilliant, far-reaching, and long-enduring, it contains the sun, moon, stars, and constellations of the zodiac, overspreading all things. Its singleness of virtue makes it Heaven. With Earth, it provides the mode of operation against which the Ruler’s institutions are presented; knowing this harmony shows knowledge of Heaven. It supports, contains, overshadows, and curtains all things, and is great because all are nourished together without injuring one another. Finally, it measures the ideal ruler and individual, whose sincerity may know its transforming and nurturing operations.

l: nature, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Nature is what Heaven has conferred; following it is the Path of duty, and fully developing it in oneself, other men, animals, and things unites external and internal.

l: the way of the superior man, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The way of the superior man is the Path of duty: an accordance with Nature whose regulation is Instruction and which cannot be left even briefly. It is a near, human path grounded in common consciousness and the ordinary intercourse of men and women, yet it reaches secretly, widely, and far through Heaven and earth beyond even the sage’s complete knowledge or practice. It unfolds by beginning with what is near and low, like traveling or ascending, rather than abandoning the right path halfway. In its fullest course, it is abundant like overflowing water, nourishing all things and rising to heaven’s height. Complete in scope, it includes the three hundred rules of ceremony and three thousand rules of demeanor, becoming fact only through perfect virtue when the proper man appears.

l: the superior man, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The superior man is a person defined by steadfast self-cultivation and faithful adherence to the Mean. He is cautious, apprehensive, and watchful over himself even when alone; he maintains friendly harmony without weakness, stands firmly in the middle, and remains unchanged whether good or bad principles prevail. Unknown or unregarded, he has no regret. He acts appropriately in every station, wealth, poverty, foreign tribes, sorrow, or difficulty, without despising inferiors, courting superiors, murmuring against Heaven, or grumbling against men. Instead, he rectifies himself, seeks the cause of failure in himself, and waits calmly for the appointments of Heaven. His growth proceeds through unceasing study, inquiry, reflection, discrimination, and practice, enabling intelligence and strength despite dullness or weakness. He values sincerity most highly, honors virtuous nature, preserves old knowledge while acquiring new knowledge, and practices propriety earnestly. In public he is humble when high and not insubordinate when low; when conditions are bad, his restraint appears through silence. Finally, he conceals virtue even as it becomes more illustrious, examines his heart, remains reverent and truthful, and influences others without rewards or anger through sincerity and reverence.

l: Equilibrium, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Equilibrium is the unstirred state of mind before pleasure, anger, sorrow, and joy arise; existing with Harmony in perfection, it roots all human actings.

l: Harmony, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Harmony is a state in which pleasure, anger, sorrow, and joy act in due degree; with Equilibrium it exists in perfection and forms the universal path all human actings should pursue.

l: world, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: A Ruler’s sincere, reverent movements illustrate institutions and become an enduring example, conducting the world toward happy tranquility.

l: Heaven and Earth, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Heaven and Earth attain happy order through perfect Equilibrium and Harmony, join sacrifices serving God, and form a ternion with one who assists their transforming and nourishing powers.

l: happy order, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: prevails_throughout heaven and earth [when Equilibrium and Harmony exist in perfection] A happy order prevails throughout heaven and earth when Equilibrium and Harmony exist in perfection, and all things are nourished and flourish.

l: Chung-ni, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Chung-ni explains how the superior man and mean man differ in relation to the course of the Mean. He then hands down Yao and Shun’s doctrines as ancestral, models Wan and Wu’s regulations, harmonizes with Heaven’s times, and conforms to water and land.

l: mean man, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The mean man lacks caution, follows dangerous paths, seeks luck and notoriety, acts against the Mean, and daily goes further to ruin.

l: the course of the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The course of the Mean is embodied and followed by the superior man, opposed by the mean man. Though people may choose it, they cannot keep it for a full month or attain it, even through difficult feats. The superior man accords with it without regret while unknown and unregarded.

l: the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The Mean is a path or course maintained by the superior man and opposed by the mean man. Most people neither walk in nor understand it: the knowing and talented go beyond it, while the stupid and worthless do not reach it. Its path is untrodden, and though men may choose it, they cannot keep to it for a full month or attain its course even amid other difficult achievements. Shun determined it from two extremes and employed it in government; Hui chose it. The superior man pursues it through learning and practice.

l: The Master, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The Master is a speaker and teacher centered on the Mean: a path he knows but says is untrodden, difficult to understand, and difficult to sustain. Perfect virtue accords with it, yet it has long been rare. Knowledgeable, talented, and virtuous people exceed it, while stupid and worthless people fall short; even those claiming wisdom cannot escape dangers or keep the Mean for a month. Though kingdoms and families may be governed, rewards declined, and weapons faced, the Mean cannot simply be attained. He contrasts southern forbearance and gentleness without revenge with northern readiness to die under arms, and urges cultivation of the proper energy. He rejects obscurity, wonders, and future honor, and says he cannot stop halfway after proceeding on the right path. The path is near ordinary human consciousness; conduct remote from it is not the path. His teaching joins reciprocity, sincerity, service, superior governance, and harmony that brings parents complete complacence. He teaches about spiritual beings, whose unseen powers enter all things and shape sacrifice. He praises Shun’s filial virtue and Heaven’s appointment, and explains the far-reaching filial piety, ceremonies, and sacrifices of King Wu and the duke of Chau. Government depends on proper people, cultivated character, duty, benevolence, preparation, sincerity, and persistent practice. He warns against ignorant judgment, unauthorized direction, and returning to antiquity. Though he can describe Hsia ceremonies imperfectly and has learned Yin ceremonies, he follows Chau ceremonies; sound and appearances are only trivial influences in transforming people.

l: perfect virtue, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: is_a the virtue according to the Mean Perfect is described as the virtue which is according to the Mean.

l: the virtue according to the Mean, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The virtue according to the Mean belongs to nature and is perfect, though rare among the people for a long time. Its greatest power unfolds through sincerity, reverence, concealment, and freedom from display, culminating in comparison with supreme Heaven’s soundless, scentless doings.

l: people, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The people rarely practice perfect virtue and have long had few who follow the Mean. They fast and purify themselves before sacrifices, then attend them. They follow only institutions, regulations, and rules that have sufficient attestation, honor, or credence. An ideal ruler inspires universal reverence, belief, pleasure, honor, and love; his lack of rewards stimulates virtue more than hatchets and battle-axes awe them.

l: flavors, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: are_distinguished_by few Flavors are eaten and drunk by everyone, but few people can distinguish them.

l: Shun, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Shun is a greatly wise, filial sage whose central practice is questioning others, studying their words, concealing bad qualities, displaying good ones, and determining and employing the Mean in governing the people. Because of great virtue, he receives Heaven’s appointment, holds the throne and riches, gains fame and long life, and has sacrifices preserved by descendants.

l: good qualities (in others), The Doctrine of the Mean
s: What was good was obtained and firmly clasped by Hui, who did not lose it.

l: government of the people, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: governs people The government of the people was conducted by Shun through his employment of the Mean.

l: men, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Men are said to be wise, yet when driven forward into nets, traps, or pitfalls, they cannot escape. Even when they choose the course of the Mean, they cannot maintain it for a full month.

l: Hui, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Hui chose the Mean, firmly holding what was good whenever he found it and never letting it go.

l: kingdom, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The kingdom, gained by King Wu, contains princes, great officers, scholars, and common people, who receive rules of royal ceremonies. Throughout it, carriages, writing, and conduct are standardized. Governed by a Ruler, it can be perfectly ruled: his institutions, acts, and words provide examples, laws, and lessons for ages, inspiring both distant longing and nearby devotion.

l: Tsze-lu, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Tsze-lu asks the Master about energy.

l: energy, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Energy is studied as southern gentleness, northern readiness to meet death, or the superior man’s firm course, which remains unchanged whether good or bad principles prevail in the country.

l: the good man, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The good man tries to follow the right path, but abandons it halfway through.

l: the sage, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The sage alone follows the course of the Mean without regret even when unknown and unregarded, though the utmost reaches of the superior man’s way remain unknown and unpracticed.

l: common men and women, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: A group may understand and practice ordinary parts of the superior man’s way, found in everyday intercourse, despite ignorance or character below the ordinary standard.

l: Earth, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Earth is large, substantial, far-reaching, and long-enduring. Its breadth and thickness sustain mountains such as Hwa and Yo and contain rivers and seas without leaking. Sharing a mode of operation with Heaven, it supports, contains, overshadows, and curtains all things. Its greatness unfolds through nourishing all things together without injury, and it is associated with the water and land to which Chung-ni conformed.

l: Book of Poetry, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Book of Poetry presents images of hawks, fishes, family, spirits, Heaven, rulers, and prudent virtue. It moves from natural and practical patterns through union, spiritual and heavenly ordinances, and praise of rulers, ending by teaching that true virtue is silent, unseen, brilliant, and unostentatious.

l: reciprocity, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: guides the principles of his nature [when they are exercised] Reciprocity is described as exercising the principles of one's nature and not doing to others what one does not like done to oneself. It is part of the way of the superior man.

l: sincerity, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Sincerity is the way of Heaven and the defining quality of the superior man, whose words and actions respect each other and avoid excess. It grounds obedience to parents, truthfulness with friends, and confidence from the sovereign. It is attained by choosing what is good and holding it firmly through study, inquiry, reflection, discrimination, earnest practice, and cultivating goodness. Complete sincerity develops one’s own nature and those of men, animals, and things, assisting Heaven and Earth. It progresses from apparent to manifest to brilliant, affects others, foreknows events, and through ceaselessness produces changes and accomplishes its ends.

l: the appointments of Heaven, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The appointment of Heaven is received by one who is greatly virtuous. The Master presents this as a certainty.

l: family, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The family is regulated through harmonious union with wife, children, and brethren; happy omens attend flourishing, unlucky omens its perishing.

l: parents, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: have_complacence entire [in such a state of things] Parents have entire complacence when there is happy union with wife and children and concord among brethren.

l: spiritual beings, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Spiritual beings are everywhere, entering all things and displaying unseen powers. They influence people’s fasting, purification, and rich sacrificial dress, appearing above and beside worshippers. Before them, the Ruler presents his institutions without doubt, a display that he knows Heaven.

l: sacrifices, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Sacrifices are attended by people who fast, purify themselves, and array themselves in their richest dresses. Spiritual beings appear to surround those attending the sacrifices.

l: sincerity, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Sincerity is an irrepressibly manifest quality, compared with the subtle yet evident presence of spiritual beings. It results from intelligence and is ascribed to nature; given sincerity, intelligence is present. It effects self-completion, is the beginning and end of things, and enables the entirely sincere man to complete himself, other men, and things.

l: Shun's virtue, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: is_a sagehood Shun's virtue was that of a sage. Because of his great virtue, he obtained the throne, riches, fame, and long life.

l: throne, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: may_be_occupied_without proper virtue [but the occupant may not make ceremonies or music] The throne was obtained by Shun because of his great virtue. Heaven is said to decree the throne as one of its favors.

l: ancestral temple, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The ancestral temple is a place for sacrifices to ancestors, whose ceremonies distinguish royal descent, rank, talents, worth, and age through ordered services.

l: King Wan, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: King Wan, son of King Chi and father of King Wu, had illustrious unceasing virtue and no cause for grief; Chau completed his virtuous course.

l: King Chi, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: lays_foundations_of King Wan's dignity King Chi was the father of King Wan. King Wu continued the enterprise of King Chi, along with that of King T'ai and King Wan.

l: King Wu, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: King Wu, son of King Wan, continues the enterprises and wishes of King T'ai, King Chi, and King Wan. He gains the kingdom and royal throne, establishes ancestral sacrifices maintained by descendants, and embodies far-reaching filial piety through carrying forward his forefathers’ undertakings.

l: duke of Chau, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The duke of Chau completes the virtuous course of Wan and Wu, gives King T'ai and King Chi the title of king, and extends royal sacrificial rules to all ranks. He establishes burial, sacrifice, and mourning rules, expressing far-reaching filial piety by carrying out forefathers’ wishes and undertakings.

l: Son of Heaven, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The Son of Heaven alone holds authority over ceremonies, measures, and written characters.

l: mourning, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Mourning durations vary by rank: one year for great officers and three for the Son of Heaven, while mourning parents equally admits no noble–mean distinction.

l: filial piety, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Filial piety skillfully carries out forefathers’ wishes and undertakings through ancestral ceremonies, offerings, music, reverence, and love.

l: forefathers, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Forefathers are served through the occupation of their places, the practice of their ceremonies, and the performance of their music. Their wishes are carried out and their undertakings are carried forward.

l: God, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: God is served by means of the ceremonies of the sacrifices to Heaven and Earth.

l: ancestors, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Ancestors receive sacrifices in the ancestral temple. They are served as the dead would have been served alive and as the departed would have been served had they continued among the living.

l: sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: serve God [through their ceremonies] The sacrifices to Heaven and Earth serve God. Understanding their ceremonies contributes to understanding how to govern a kingdom.

l: sacrifices to ancestors, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: sacrifice_to ancestors [through their ceremonies] The sacrifices to ancestors are performed through the ceremonies of the ancestral temple. Understanding their meaning contributes to understanding how to govern a kingdom.

l: government of a kingdom, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: is_a easy to look into one's palm [for one who understands the ceremonies of sacrifices to Heaven and Earth and the meaning of sacrifices to ancestors] The government of a kingdom is said to be as easy as looking into one’s palm for someone who understands the ceremonies of the sacrifices to Heaven and Earth and the meaning of the sacrifices to ancestors.

l: kingdom, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Kingdom is a place whose governance may be well or ill governed; it unfolds from ease through sacrificial understanding to rule by cultivated character, proper men, and nine standard rules.

l: government, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Government flourishes with proper men and decays without them; administration depends on the ruler’s character, duty, and benevolence to obtain them.

l: men, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: are_obtained_through ruler [through the ruler's own character] Men are necessary for government to flourish. Proper men are obtained through the ruler’s cultivated character, and men of virtue and talents are encouraged by honor and material support.

l: ruler, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The ruler cultivates character through duty, serves parents, acquires knowledge of men, and knows Heaven. As sovereign, he governs kingdom, states, and families by nine standard rules, honoring virtue, treating people kindly, and cherishing princes.

l: character and conduct, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Character is cultivated by treading in the ways of duty. The ruler’s character establishes the duties of universal obligation.

l: duty, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: is_cultivated_by benevolence [through treading its ways] Duty is cultivated through the cherishing of benevolence. The ways of duty can be known naturally, through study, or after painful ignorance, and practiced with natural ease, desire for advantage, or strenuous effort.

l: benevolence, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Benevolence is humanity’s characteristic element, chiefly exercised through loving relatives.

l: propriety, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: produces the decreasing measures of the love due to relatives [and the steps in the honor due to the worthy] Propriety produces the decreasing measures of love due to relatives and the steps in honor due to the worthy. A ruler cultivates his person by avoiding movements contrary to the rules of propriety.

l: knowledge, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Knowledge, a universally binding virtue belonging to nature, requires Heaven and is shown by other men; learning, inquiry, reflection, discrimination, and practice lead toward it.

l: the five universal duties, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The five universal duties are obligations between sovereign and minister, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger brother, and friends.

l: the three universal virtues, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: is_a three universally binding virtues The three universal virtues are knowledge, magnanimity, and energy. They are universally binding and are carried into practice through singleness.

l: singleness, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: is_the_means_by_which the five universal duties [they are carried into practice] Singleness is the means by which the three universal virtues carry the five universal duties into practice. It is also the means by which the nine standard rules are put into effect.

l: learning, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: is_near_to knowledge [being fond of learning] Learning brings a person near to knowledge. The superior man continues learning and laboring until nothing remains unstudied or misunderstood.

l: states and families, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: States and families are governed through the nine standard rules. The rules include affection toward relatives and kindly cherishing the princes of the states, including restoring broken families and reviving extinguished states.

l: the nine standard rules, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The nine standard rules are practices pursued by singleness: cultivating one’s character, honoring virtue and talent, caring for relatives, ministers, officers, and people, encouraging artisans, treating distant men indulgently, and cherishing princes of the states.

l: the way of men, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: is_the_attainment_of sincerity The way of men is the attainment of sincerity. It belongs to the person who chooses what is good and firmly holds it fast.

l: intelligence, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Intelligence results from sincerity, is ascribed to instruction, and reciprocally entails sincerity.

l: nature, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Nature is associated with sincerity that results from intelligence.

l: instruction, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Instruction is associated with intelligence that results from sincerity.

l: the transforming and nourishing powers of Heaven and Earth, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: are_powers_of Heaven and Earth [transforming and nourishing] The transforming and nourishing powers of Heaven and Earth can be assisted by one who fully develops the natures of creatures and things.

l: person (the cultivator of goodness), The Doctrine of the Mean
s: A person cultivates goodness to its utmost, attains complete sincerity, and thereby gains the capacity to transform others under heaven.

l: others, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Others are changed and transformed by the brilliance of sincerity.

l: happy omens, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Happy omens, seen in milfoil, tortoise, and four-limb movements, appear before a nation or family flourishes.

l: unlucky omens, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: affect movements of the four limbs [as such events] Unlucky omens appear when a nation or family is about to perish.

l: calamity, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Calamity can be foreknown before it arrives.

l: happiness, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Happiness can be foreknown before it arrives.

l: individual possessed of the most complete sincerity, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: An individual of complete sincerity, like a spirit, foreknows approaching happiness and calamity, revealing knowledge of both good and evil.

l: spirit, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: is_approached_to in silence [during the offering] The spirit is used as a likeness for the individual possessed of the most complete sincerity.

l: self-completion, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: shows perfect virtue [as the completing himself] Self-completion is effected by sincerity. The entirely sincere man’s self-completion shows his perfect virtue.

l: the way, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: directs man [as the means by which man must direct himself] The way is that by which man must direct himself. It is also the way by which a union of the external and internal is effected.

l: ceaselessness, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Ceaselessness continues long and reaches far, becoming large, substantial, high, and brilliant; it contains, overspreads, and perfects all things through its unceasing singleness.

l: individual possessed of the most entire sincerity, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: An individual possessing the most entire sincerity is portrayed as large and substantial like Earth, high and brilliant like Heaven, and infinite in reach and duration. With all Heavenly virtue, quick apprehension, clear discernment, far-reaching intelligence, and all-embracing knowledge, he can regulate mankind’s enduring relations, establish humanity’s fundamental virtues, and understand Heaven and Earth’s transforming, nurturing operations. He unfolds as earnest in ideal, abyss-deep, Heaven-vast, and dependent on nothing beyond himself.

l: the way of Heaven and Earth, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The way of Heaven and Earth, without doubleness, unfathomably produces things and is large, substantial, high, brilliant, far-reaching, and long-enduring.

l: sun, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The sun shines successively, illuminating wherever sun and moon shine, while pursuing its course without colliding with the moon.

l: moon, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The moon shines successively, compared to Chung-ni, following its course without colliding with the sun.

l: ceremonies, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Ceremonies may be made only by one who has proper virtue and occupies the throne; virtue without the throne or the throne without proper virtue is insufficient.

l: virtue, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: may_exist_without throne [but its possessor may not presume to make ceremonies or music] Proper virtue is required for a person who occupies the throne to make ceremonies or music. Possessing virtue without occupying the throne does not permit a person to presume to make them.

l: music, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Music, like ceremonies, may be made only by one who has proper virtue and occupies the throne.

l: Chau, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Chau is the dynasty whose ceremonies are now used, and the Master follows them.

l: ceremonies of Chau, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: are_used now The ceremonies of Chau are now in use, and the Master follows them.

l: Ruler, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Ruler is a sovereign whose institutions rest on character and conduct. By testing them, knowing Heaven, and awaiting a sage, he reduces errors in government. From sovereignty and three important things, his movements become lasting examples, his acts laws, and his words lessons for the kingdom.

l: regulations, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: Regulations from former times lack credence when unattested; those made by someone inferior cannot be honored, so people do not follow them.

l: institutions, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The Ruler’s institutions rest on character and conduct, are attested by the people, conform to Heaven and Earth, and are accepted by spiritual beings. Compared with the three kings and enduring without misgivings, they await confirmation from a sage a hundred ages later.

l: sage, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: is_a future wise ruler [arising a hundred ages after] The Ruler is prepared to wait for the rise of a sage a hundred ages after without misgivings. This readiness is part of the testing and confidence surrounding his institutions.

l: four seasons, The Doctrine of the Mean
s: have_alternating_progress alternating progress [in comparison to Chung-ni] The four seasons are compared to Chung-ni in their alternating progress. Their courses are pursued without collision among them.

l: ruler (ideal sage), The Doctrine of the Mean
s: The ideal ruler possesses every sagely quality: clear, far-reaching intelligence; vast knowledge; magnanimity, generosity, firmness, and discrimination. Self-adjusted and grave, he never swerves from the Mean and commands reverence. Like Heaven in vastness and an abyss in depth, he sends forth virtues in season; they spread through the Middle Kingdom and to barbarous tribes, where all honor and love him as the equal of Heaven.

l: Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: This unit is Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), translated by James Legge, and consists of Mencius’s counsel to rulers on benevolence, righteousness, and royal government. It begins with King Hui of Liang seeking profit, but Mencius insists that a kingdom must be guided by benevolence and righteousness rather than competition for gain. Through discussions of royal possessions, famine, taxes, warfare, and defeat, he argues that rulers who neglect hungry people are responsible for their suffering, while light burdens, secure livelihoods, education, and moral cultivation can win popular support and make a ruler invincible. Mencius similarly tells King Xiang of Liang that unity under one sway will follow a ruler who does not delight in killing. The central extended exchange is with King Xuan of Qi. Mencius identifies the king’s compassion for an ox as evidence that he can protect his people if he extends that feeling beyond animals. He repeatedly teaches that a ruler’s music, parks, wealth, beauty, tours, hunting, and joy must be shared with the people rather than purchased through their distress. He defines royal government as protecting livelihoods and the destitute, educating people in filial and fraternal duties, appointing and dismissing officials responsibly, and acting with the people’s judgment in serious cases. He rejects war as the means to Qi’s ambitions and distinguishes a true sovereign from a robber or ruffian who violates benevolence and righteousness. When Qi conquers Yan, Mencius makes possession conditional on Yan’s people’s approval and urges restoration, consultation, and withdrawal when Qi’s conduct provokes opposition. The later chapters extend these principles to Duke Mu, Duke Wen of Teng, and Duke Ping of Lu. Mencius explains that people will not defend officers who ignored their earlier misery, advises small Teng to prepare its defenses while pursuing goodness, and presents King Tai’s migration as an example of responding to necessity. The work ends with Meng Ke learning that Zang Cang prevented Duke Ping from visiting him; he accepts that Heaven determines whether a ruler will trust and employ him.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Mencius is a teacher, scholar, adviser, counsellor, and venerable Sir whose sole counsels concern benevolence and righteousness. He repeatedly advises rulers that true royal government depends on caring for the people: sharing pleasures rather than enjoying possessions alone, preventing hunger, lightening taxes and punishments, supporting farming and education, and giving people secure livelihoods. Beginning with King Hui of Liang, he rejects profit as the ruler’s central concern, criticizes famine amid abundance in the ruler’s household, and argues that even a small territory can attain royal dignity through benevolent government. He then judges rulers by their willingness to avoid killing and unite the kingdom under humane rule. With King Xuan of Qi, he develops these counsels through compassion, shared music and parks, proper treatment of states, worthy ministers, public judgment, and restraint in conquest. He explains that Zhou was cut off as a fellow who violated benevolence and righteousness, not as a sovereign put to death. In advice concerning Yan, he makes the people’s pleasure decisive and urges restoration, consultation, withdrawal, and benevolent government after harmful conduct. He also counsels Duke Mu and Duke Wen of Teng about famine, defense, threatened fortifications, doing good, and accepting Heaven’s ultimate determination. At the end, when a planned visit from Duke Ping of Lu is prevented, he concludes that Heaven determines whether he will find a suitable ruler.

l: Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: A book translated by James Legge, consisting of Part I.

l: King Hui of Liang, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: King Hui of Liang is a king and prince who rules and administers Liang’s kingdom, seeking Mencius’s counsel on how to profit it. He is concerned with governing, says he exerts his mind fully during bad years by moving people and grain, and wonders why his population does not grow. Yet he has small virtue: while his pond holds large geese and deer and his kitchen and stables are supplied, his people suffer hunger. Mencius challenges his pleasure in possessions, his treatment of famine as the year’s fault, and the violence inflicted through government, likening it to killing. Hui is also fond of war and, after Jin’s defeats, his eldest son’s death, territorial loss, and disgrace to his departed predecessors, asks for a course to erase that shame once for all.

l: profit, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Profit is a dangerous guiding concern: putting it before righteousness endangers the kingdom as superiors and inferiors compete to snatch gain.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_a counsel [provided by Mencius] Benevolence is presented as a central topic for governing. A benevolent man does not neglect his parents.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Righteousness, Mencius’s counsel, comes before profit; when profit is first it is last, and sovereigns are not afterthoughts.

l: kingdom (King Hui of Liang's kingdom), Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: King Hui of Liang's kingdom contains great officers and people, governed through moving people and conveying grain in bad years. It is endangered when profit is prioritized over righteousness; benevolence and righteousness should guide it, yet its people do not increase while animals consume human food.

l: putting a sovereign to death, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: results_in families [a family of a thousand chariots for the murderer] Putting a sovereign to death is raised by king Xuan of Qi as a question about whether a minister may do so. Mencius says he has not heard of putting a sovereign to death in the case of Zhou.

l: Book of Poetry, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: A book recounting King Wen’s marvellous tower and pond, citing poetry on misery, solitude, Gong Liu, and king Tai.

l: king Wen, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: King Wen is portrayed as a marvellous ruler whose tower, pond, park, animals, birds, fish, and turtles share an image of abundance. His seventy-square-li park was open to grass-cutters, fuel-gatherers, and hunters, showing that he shared it with the people. He served the Kun barbarians despite commanding a great country, practised true royal government, and showed valour by stopping the march to Chu, consolidating Zhou’s prosperity, meeting the nation’s expectations, and giving repose to the kingdom’s people. His benevolent government prioritized four destitute classes, limited taxes and prohibitions, protected criminals’ families from inherited guilt, and did not take possession without the people’s approval.

l: Tang, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Tang, a prince ruling a seventy-li kingdom, begins administering justice at Ge; the people trust him and welcome his progress.

l: the people, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The people eagerly built King Wen’s marvellous tower in less than a day, rejoicing in the tower and pond and sharing pleasure in his deer, fish, and turtles. Their response portrays them figuratively as King Wen’s children, unlike their wish for Jie’s death.

l: tower (King Wen's tower), Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_a marvellous tower King Wen measured out, planned, and began building his marvellous tower with the strength of the people. The people willingly worked on it and called it the marvellous tower.

l: park (King Wen's park), Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: King Wen’s seventy-square-li park was shared with people, granting grass-cutters, fuel-gatherers, and pheasant and hare catchers entry privileges.

l: pond (King Wen's pond), Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_a marvellous pond King Wen made his marvellous pond with the strength of the people. The people willingly worked on it, called it the marvellous pond, and rejoiced in its fish.

l: pleasure, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_shared_by the people [by wise and good rulers] Wise and good princes can enjoy their towers, ponds, birds, and animals because their people have pleasure in them as well. A ruler who lacks the people's support cannot enjoy such things alone.

l: people (King Hui of Liang's kingdom), Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: King Hui of Liang's people are moved and fed grain in bad years, yet remain no more numerous than neighboring kingdoms. They visibly suffer hunger and die of famine while the king keeps fat meat and horses. Mencius says sound management of resources, land, and education would bring prosperity.

l: neighboring kingdoms, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The neighboring kingdoms, judged by King Hui of Liang, have princes less diligent than he is, yet their people do not decrease while his kingdom’s people do not increase.

l: war, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: has_soldiers soldiers War provides Mencius with an illustration of rulers' limited efforts. Soldiers advance to drums, then some run fifty paces and others one hundred, though all have run away.

l: seasons of husbandry, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: should_not_be_interfered_with grain production If the seasons of husbandry are not interfered with, grain will be more than can be eaten.

l: grain, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_more_than_can_be_eaten more than can be eaten [when seasons of husbandry are not interfered with] Grain is conveyed to parts of the kingdom during bad years. When the seasons of husbandry are not interfered with, it becomes more than can be eaten.

l: benevolent government, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Benevolent government is royal government based on love and protection of the people. It begins by enabling people to nourish the living and bury the dead without resentment, through proper resource management and education. It uses light taxes, levies, punishments, and fines; careful cultivation of fields; support for families; and teaching filial piety, fraternal respectfulness, sincerity, and truthfulness. When good government is lacking, the king does not answer what should be done. If duke Mu practices it, the people will love him, those above them, and die for their officers.

l: silk, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Silk is clothing for people of fifty and grey-haired elders when mulberry trees surround homesteads, signifying prosperity associated with royal dignity.

l: education in schools, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Education in schools under benevolent government receives careful attention and especially inculcates filial and fraternal duties.

l: filial and fraternal duties, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Filial and fraternal duties should be especially taught in schools, ensuring grey-haired elders need not carry burdens on roads.

l: grey-haired elders, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Grey-haired elders benefit when livelihood and education are well regulated, enjoying silk and flesh under benevolent government instead of carrying burdens on roads.

l: royal dignity, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Royal dignity is a status attainable through benevolent rule. It is reached when a ruler ensures elderly people wear silk and eat flesh, the black-haired people lack neither hunger nor cold, and the ruler shares the people’s joy and sorrow. Even if a duke merely does good, a descendant in a later generation may attain it.

l: people dying from famine, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: are_on roads People dying from famine are described as lying on the roads while King Hui of Liang does not issue grain from his granaries for them.

l: famine, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Famine kills people on the roads, among the people of Liang, and in the wilds. As King Hui of Liang leaves stored grain unissued, Mencius cites the suffering and deaths to condemn his government.

l: year, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_blamed_for people dying from famine [by the king] King Hui of Liang blames the year when people die, saying their deaths are not owing to him. Mencius tells him to stop laying the blame on the year.

l: nation, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: sends people [to King Hui of Liang when he ceases blaming the year] Mencius says that if King Hui of Liang stops blaming the year, people from all the nation will instantly come to him.

l: beasts, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: devour men Beasts devour one another, and men hate them for doing so. Mencius compares a ruler who causes people to die of hunger to one who leads beasts to devour men.

l: government, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_equivalent_to sword [as a means of killing a man] Government can cause killing when it is administered so that people are led to die of hunger. Mencius says this form of government is no different from killing with a sword.

l: Jin, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Jin, once the nation’s strongest state, declines under King Hui of Liang through defeat by Qi, territorial loss to Qin, and disgrace by Chu.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Qi is a small, narrow State and kingdom, one of the nine divisions, yet is regarded as strong. It has defined borders and is one of the kingdoms near Teng. Mencius inquires into its prohibitory regulations on arriving there and presents its government under king Wen as an example of true royal government. Qi could approach good government if its king shared his great love of music with the people. It defeats Jin in the east, after which King Hui of Liang’s eldest son perishes. Qi then attacks, conquers, smites, and takes possession of Yan, doubling its territory; but its treatment of Yan and lack of benevolent government lead other princes to plan an attack.

l: Qin, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: takes Jin's territorial loss to Qin [seven hundred li of territory on the west] Qin took seven hundred li of territory from Jin. Mencius says Qin's ruler robs the people of their time and drives them into hardship.

l: Chu, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Chu is a great country and power south of Jin, contrasted with the smaller Zou. It disgraces Jin, and its ruler burdens the people through hardship. As Teng lies between kingdoms, Duke Wen considers whether Teng should serve Chu.

l: the people of Qin and Chu, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The people of Qin and Chu lose time for ploughing and weeding because of their rulers; their parents suffer cold and hunger and families scatter. Though they serve fathers, brothers, elders, and superiors with respect, Qin and Chu troops can be opposed with sticks.

l: the rulers of Qin and Chu, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The rulers of Qin and Chu are depicted as robbing their people of time needed for farming, causing cold and hunger among parents, separating families by driving people abroad, and treating the people as though driving them into pit-falls or drowning.

l: territory of Jin, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: has_extent seven hundred li [lost to Qin on the west] Seven hundred li of Jin's territory was lost to Qin.

l: the saying 'The benevolent has no enemy', Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: states benevolent rule's lack of enemies The saying 'The benevolent has no enemy' is presented as supporting Mencius's advice to King Hui of Liang.

l: Jin's defeat by Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: occurs on the east [after King Hui of Liang inherited Jin] Jin was defeated by Qi in the east after King Hui of Liang inherited the state.

l: the death of King Hui's eldest son, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: occurs after Jin's defeat by Qi King Hui of Liang's eldest son perished after Jin was defeated by Qi.

l: Jin's territorial loss to Qin, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: occurs on the west [seven hundred li of territory] Jin lost seven hundred li of territory to Qin.

l: Jin's disgrace at the hands of Chu, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: occurs on the south Jin sustained disgrace at the hands of Chu.

l: King Hui's wish to wipe away the shame, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: concerns King Hui's departed predecessors [once for all] King Hui of Liang wishes to wipe away the shame brought on his departed predecessors by Jin's setbacks.

l: benevolent rule's lack of enemies, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Benevolent rule, said to have no enemy, enables royal dignity through benevolent government.

l: king Xiang of Liang, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: King Xiang of Liang asks Mencius how to settle the kingdom; Mencius rebukes his lack of sovereign, venerable bearing.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_settled_by one sway [when united under it] The kingdom could be settled by being united under one sway.

l: one sway, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: One sway is the condition under which the kingdom would be settled. Mencius said it could be established by one who had no pleasure in killing men.

l: all the people of the nation, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: All the people of the nation would unanimously give the kingdom to one who has no pleasure in killing men, look toward him with outstretched necks, and flock to him as water flows downward with a rush.

l: shepherds of men throughout the nation, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: find_pleasure killing men [every one of them] The shepherds of men throughout the nation all took pleasure in killing men. Mencius said that if one of them did not take pleasure in killing men, all the people would turn toward him.

l: one who has no pleasure in killing men, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: A shepherd of men who rejects killing could unite the kingdom, gaining irresistible support as all the nation flocks to him.

l: Chapter 7, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_a chapter Chapter 7 records Mencius’s conversation with King Xuan of Qi about royal government, royal sway, benevolence, and the livelihood of the people.

l: king Xuan of Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: King Xuan of Qi is the king of Qi, a ruler who seeks to enlarge his territories and rule the Middle Kingdom, often through war. Across repeated interviews with Mencius, he asks about royal government, royal sway, relations with neighbouring kingdoms, ministers, ability, punishment, conquest, and threats to Qi. He displays compassion toward an ox, which Mencius treats as evidence of compassion sufficient to reach animals, and he is told he can attain royal sway if he extends concern to his people. His tastes and infirmities include present-age music, hunting, valour, wealth, and beauty. Mencius repeatedly connects these pleasures to government: the king can gain royal sway by sharing pleasure with the people and can attain true royal government by enabling them to gratify their own love of wealth and beauty. The king also considers his park, the Hall of Distinction, and pleasure in the Snow palace. Though he can judge that neglectful friends, incapable judges, and unregulated officers should be removed, he evades a question about the lack of good government in his kingdom. Later, he asks how to judge and appoint men, whether ministers may kill sovereigns, and whether Qi should take Yan. Mencius warns that possession of Yan depends on Yan’s people being pleased, and advises restoring captives, ceasing removal of precious vessels, consulting Yan’s people about a ruler, and withdrawing to avert attack and calamity.

l: royal sway, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Royal sway depends on loving and protecting the people. Mencius says King Xuan of Qi can attain it by extending kindness, instituting benevolent government, and sharing pleasure with the people.

l: love and protection of the people, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Love and protection of the people are identified as the virtue needed for royal sway. Mencius says King Xuan of Qi’s kindness must be extended from animals to the people.

l: people of Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The people of Qi are a people whose responses reveal the condition of their rule. They hear the king’s music and see his hunting; they complain when these pleasures bring distress, separation, and scattering, but rejoice when they signal his freedom from sickness. Lacking a secure livelihood, they may fall into moral deflection and depravity; benevolent government would support their families. They attack and conquer Yan, then plan to fortify Xue, alarming duke Wen of Teng.

l: the incident of the ox and the bell, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: King Xuan of Qi releases a frightened ox before bell consecration and substitutes a sheep. Mencius interprets the change as compassion for what the king saw, rather than reluctance to bear expense.

l: ox, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The ox was being led to have its blood used to consecrate a bell. King Xuan of Qi ordered it released because he could not bear seeing it go innocently to the place of death.

l: sheep, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The sheep was ordered in place of the ox for the consecration of the bell. Mencius says the king had seen the ox but had not seen the sheep, explaining the difference in his response.

l: compassion, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: supports royal sway [when extended to the people] Compassion is shown in King Xuan of Qi’s inability to bear the sight of the ox being led to death. Mencius says such compassion can be extended from animals to the people.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_a artifice Benevolence is shown by King Xuan of Qi’s conduct toward the ox and is described as an artifice of benevolence. Mencius says a prince who carries out his benevolent heart can secure the love and protection of all within the four seas.

l: Zou, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Zou is involved in a brush with Lu.

l: the Middle Kingdom, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_a realm The Middle Kingdom is among King Xuan of Qi’s stated desires. He wishes to rule it, have Qin and Chu wait at his court, enlarge his territories, and attract the surrounding barbarous tribes.

l: war, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: War is associated with collecting military equipment, endangering soldiers and officers, and provoking resentment among other princes. Mencius says pursuing King Xuan of Qi’s desires through such actions is like climbing a tree to seek for fish and will bring calamities.

l: intelligent ruler, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: An intelligent ruler secures people’s livelihoods so families endure good and bad years, then establishes schooling emphasizing filial and fraternal duties to guide them toward goodness.

l: people of Chu, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The people of Chu are used in Mencius’s example of a conflict between the people of Zou and the people of Chu. King Xuan of Qi agrees that the people of Chu would conquer, illustrating that the strong overcome the weak.

l: livelihood of the people, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: provides service to parents [when properly regulated] The livelihood of the people should be regulated so that families have enough to serve parents and support wives and children. Mencius recommends mulberry-trees, properly timed breeding of animals, uninterrupted farming, and education to secure this livelihood.

l: music, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Music, whether present-day or ancient, has the same effect on good government. The king prefers music of the present age, while Mencius stresses that shared enjoyment, especially with many, is more pleasant than enjoying it alone or with few.

l: government of the State, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Good government is said to be near when the king has a very great love of music, provided that his pleasure is shared with the people. In the government of the State, the king tells a learned man to set aside what he has learned and follow him. Mencius presents this as inconsistent with the king's conduct toward valuable materials and skilled craftsmanship.

l: hunting, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The king's hunting causes the people distress when they hear his carriages and horses and see his plumes and streamers while families are separated and scattered. The people respond joyfully when the hunting appears to show that the king is free from sickness.

l: ancient sovereigns, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The ancient sovereigns toured and surveyed the States, examined spring ploughing and autumn reaping, supplied lacking seed or yield, and avoided pleasures of yielding to the current, wildness, or being lost.

l: king Xuan's park, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: King Xuan's forty-square-li park, inside barrier-gates, made killing a deer punishable as killing a man.

l: people, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: A group judges parks by shared access: king Wen’s larger park seems small, while king Xuan’s restricted smaller park seems large.

l: pitfall, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_in kingdom of Qi [in the middle of the kingdom] The forty-square-li park is described as a pitfall in the middle of the kingdom because killing a deer there is treated as killing a person.

l: maintenance of intercourse with neighbouring kingdoms, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_a way [for regulating one's intercourse with neighbouring kingdoms] Maintenance of intercourse with neighbouring kingdoms requires a perfectly virtuous prince to serve a small country with a great country, or a wise prince to serve a large country with a small country. These forms of conduct are presented as delighting in or standing in awe of Heaven.

l: king Tai, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: King Tai is a king, described as fond of beauty and loving the lady of Jiang; together they chose a settlement site. He formerly dwelt in Bin, where he served the barbarians of the north with gifts, yet their repeated incursions continued. Regarded by the people of Pin as a benevolent man, he left Bin to preserve his people when the barbarians sought his territory. After crossing mountain Liang, he built a town and established his residence at the foot of mount Qi, where he dwelt.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Heaven produces inferior people and makes rulers and teachers for them. It is tied to proper conduct between great and small states: delight in it brings love and protection to the whole kingdom, while awe brings these to one kingdom. Heaven determines accomplishment of the great result and whether Meng Ke finds a ruler who trusts and practices his counsels.

l: valour, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Valour can be small, like a common man brandishing his sword and challenging a single opponent, or great, like the valour of king Wen and king Wu. Great valour is shown by using anger to give repose to all the people of the kingdom.

l: the people of the kingdom, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The people of the kingdom receive repose when a ruler displays the greater valour exemplified by king Wen and king Wu. Mencius says that they fear king Xuan of Qi does not love the valour that would bring them such repose.

l: king Wu, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: King Wu, valourous and ashamed of violence and disorder, acted when the people were pleased; one display of his anger gave repose to all the people of the kingdom.

l: men of talents and worth, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Talents and virtue are qualities considered when deciding whether to appoint a man. The ruler should not accept private or official claims about them without investigation, but should examine the case when all the people make the claim.

l: the people, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The people suffer under rulers whose tours exhaust provisions and impose ceaseless toil, yet they share a ruler’s joy and sorrow when he shares their condition. They should be enabled to gratify wealth and beauty; king Wen advanced welfare through provisions, protection, and care for the destitute.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Kingdom is defined by shared joy or sorrow between ruler and people, enabling the ruler to attain royal dignity.

l: duke Jing of Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: has_minister minister Yan Duke Jing of Qi asked minister Yan how to make his visit to Zhuan Fu, Chao Wu, and Lang Xie comparable to the inspection tours of ancient sovereigns. Pleased by Yan's answer, he proclaimed throughout his State, occupied a shed in the borders, opened his granaries to supply the people, and commissioned music for a prince and minister pleased with each other.

l: minister Yan, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: advises duke Jing of Qi [about his tour of inspection] Minister Yan explained to duke Jing of Qi that ancient royal inspections and reports of office had purposes connected with surveying administration and supplying deficiencies in seed or yield. He warned against oppressive processions, uncontrolled pleasures, and rulers who yield to or press against the current without returning.

l: tour of inspection, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_a visit of inspection [by the Son of Heaven among the States] A tour of inspection was the name for the Son of Heaven's visit to the princes to survey the States under their care. Its proper purposes included examining ploughing and reaping and supplying deficiencies, rather than consuming provisions and oppressing the people.

l: princes, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: report administration of their offices [at the court of the Son of Heaven] Princes were visited by the Son of Heaven during a tour of inspection and attended the Son of Heaven's court for a report of office. The ancient sovereigns' conduct was described as a pattern for the princes.

l: joy, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: When a ruler rejoices in the joy of his people, the people rejoice in his joy. A sympathy of joy can spread throughout the kingdom.

l: sorrow, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: When a ruler grieves at the sorrow of his people, the people grieve at his sorrow. A sympathy of sorrow can spread throughout the kingdom.

l: Hall of Distinction, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_a Hall appropriate to the sovereigns The Hall of Distinction is described by Mencius as a hall appropriate to the sovereigns. King Xuan of Qi is asked whether it should be pulled down.

l: true royal government, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: requires_preserving Hall of Distinction True royal government is presented as benevolent government that protects the people, gives attention first to the most destitute, and allows the people to satisfy their desires for wealth and beauty.

l: Gong Liu, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Gong Liu, formerly fond of wealth, builds ricks and granaries, provides provisions for those staying and marching, then gathers his people and begins a march.

l: four classes of destitute people, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The four classes of destitute people, the old without wives, husbands, or children, and the young without fathers, lack anyone to tell their wants and are king Wen’s first objects of benevolent government.

l: wealth, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Wealth is a desire that king Xuan of Qi admits having. Mencius says that Gong Liu also loved wealth and argues that the king should give the people power to gratify the same feeling.

l: beauty, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Beauty is a desire that king Xuan of Qi admits having. Mencius says that king Tai loved beauty and argues that the king should let the people gratify the same feeling.

l: government, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Government provides land shares, protects the destitute, supports people, regulates commerce without taxing goods, permits ponds and weirs, and limits criminals’ guilt to themselves.

l: minister (king Xuan of Qi's minister), Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: has_family wife and children (the minister's family) The minister entrusts his wife and children to the care of his friend while he travels into Chu.

l: friend (the minister's friend), Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The friend is said to have let the minister’s wife and children suffer from cold and hunger. The king says that such a friend should be cast off.

l: chief criminal judge (king Xuan of Qi's chief criminal judge), Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The chief criminal judge is described as unable to regulate the officers under him. The king says that he should be dismissed.

l: kingdom (king Xuan of Qi's kingdom), Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: lacks good government (the kingdom's government) [within the four borders of the kingdom] Mencius asks what should be done if there is not good government within the kingdom’s four borders.

l: the interview between Mencius and king Xuan of Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Mencius advises king Xuan of Qi on ancient kingdoms, ministers, and officeholders, emphasizing investigation of the people's opinions before action.

l: ministers, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: are_sprung_from families noted for generations [in an ancient kingdom] Ministers in an ancient kingdom are sprung from families noted in it for generations. King Xuan of Qi is told that he has no intimate ministers, and those he advanced yesterday may be gone today without his knowing it.

l: people, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The people judge whether a candidate for office has talent and virtue, will not do, or deserves death; the ruler must investigate their judgment before appointing, dismissing, or executing him.

l: candidate for office, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: has talents and virtue [when fit for advancement to office] A candidate for office may be advanced when the people judge him to have talents and virtue, but the ruler must first examine the case. If the ruler finds that the candidate will not do, he should send him away.

l: death, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Death is considered when all the people say that a man deserves it. The ruler must inquire into the case and put the man to death only when he sees that the man deserves death.

l: the killing of the candidate by the people, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_a killing The saying "The people killed him" describes the outcome when the people all say that a man deserves death, the ruler investigates, and the ruler finds that the man deserves death.

l: cutting off the fellow Zhou, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Mencius says he has heard of the cutting off of the fellow Zhou. He distinguishes this from putting a sovereign to death.

l: man, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: A man spends his youth learning principles of right government; grown vigorous, he wishes to practice them, but the king commands him to set them aside and follow.

l: principles of right government, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The principles of right government are studied by a man during his youth. When he is grown and wishes to apply them, the king tells him to put them aside for the present.

l: gem, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: has_value 240,000 taels The gem is unwrought in the stone and is said to be worth 240,000 taels. The king would employ a lapidary to cut and polish it.

l: Yan, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Yan is a kingdom and State conquered and occupied by Qi after its ruler tyrannized its people; Qi considered popular approval, then dismantled Yan’s ancestral temple and removed its precious vessels.

l: the people of Yan, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The people of Yan welcomed King Xuan’s host with baskets of rice and vessels of congee, hoping to escape fire and water and gain liberation from Yan’s ruler. Their hopes failed as they suffered killings, confinement, and destruction of their ancestral temple. Mencius warned that, if water became deeper and fire fiercer, they would make another revolution.

l: the conquest of Yan by Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Qi’s conquest of Yan, an achievement beyond mere human strength, took fifty days. It began as punishment of Yan’s tyrannical ruler but became a violent occupation; whether Qi could retain Yan depended on Yan’s people welcoming it.

l: the princes of the various States, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The princes of various States deliberate after Qi takes Yan, resolve to free Yan, and threaten attack, prompting King Xuan to seek Mencius’s advice.

l: barbarians of the north, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The barbarians of the north continually made incursions into Bin while Tang was engaged in the south, causing suffering despite receiving skins, silks, dogs, horses, pearls, and gems from king Tai.

l: the ruler of Yan, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: tyrannizes the people of Yan The ruler of Yan is described as having tyrannized over his people. King Xuan went to punish him, but Mencius said Qi’s subsequent actions were improper.

l: the princes' threatened attack on Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_planned_by the princes of the various States The princes’ threatened attack on Qi arose after Qi took possession of Yan and failed to practice benevolent government. Mencius said the rest of the kingdom was jealously afraid of Qi’s strength and was moved to arms by its conduct.

l: Qi's punitive expedition against Yan, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Qi attacked Yan over its ruler’s tyranny, but hoped-for deliverance became further abuses under Qi’s control.

l: benevolent government, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_absent_from Qi [after the conquest of Yan] Mencius said that Qi’s doubled territory was not accompanied by benevolent government. He presented benevolent rule as necessary to prevent the other states from attacking Qi.

l: the restoration of the captives and withdrawal from Yan, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Mencius advises King Xuan to restore captives, cease taking Yan’s vessels, consult its people on a ruler, and withdraw, possibly averting princes’ attack on Qi.

l: Lu, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Lu is involved in a brush with Zou.

l: brush between Zou and Lu, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_a conflict The brush between Zou and Lu provides the setting for duke Mu's question to Mencius.

l: duke Mu, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_a duke Duke Mu tells Mencius that thirty-three of his officers were killed and that none of the people defended them. He asks how to address the people's conduct when punishing all of them seems impossible.

l: officers, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Duke Mu's thirty-three officers are killed after failing to report the people's suffering despite full state stores and arsenals.

l: people, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The people suffer in calamitous and famine years: the old and weak are abandoned, while the able-bodied scatter. Mencius says they repay their officers’ conduct and would die for them under benevolent government.

l: duke Wen of Teng, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Duke Wen of Teng rules and guards Teng and its people amid pressure from the large kingdoms Qi and Chu. Seeking Mencius’s guidance, he considers serving either power to protect Teng, worries over Qi’s fortification of Xue, and asks how Teng can avoid suffering. Mencius urges stronger defenses, readiness to die defending Teng, and strength in doing good, while presenting two possible courses through king Tai’s example.

l: Teng, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Teng is a small kingdom or State between Qi and Chu, with large kingdoms on both sides. Though it serves them, it suffers from them. Its moats and walls matter because Teng is advised to strengthen defenses and prepare for attack.

l: the people of Teng, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: The people of Teng are guarded and kept with duke Wen, prepared to remain and defend Teng if it is attacked.

l: serving Qi or Chu, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_a plan [proposed by duke Wen of Teng] Serving Qi or Chu is the choice Duke Wen of Teng asks Mencius to address. Mencius says the proposed plan is beyond him and instead recommends strengthening Teng's defenses.

l: attack on Teng, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: threatens Teng [in case of attack] In case of attack, Mencius advises Teng to have deeper moats, higher walls, strong guards, and people prepared to remain and die in its defense.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Qi is associated with the people who are going to fortify Xue. Mencius says that Qi is not the duke’s concern compared with doing good.

l: Xue, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Xue is the place that the people of Qi are going to fortify.

l: fortification of Xue, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: is_a fortification It is the threatened action that occasions duke Wen of Teng great alarm.

l: Bin, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang)
s: Bin was the place where king Tai dwelt before the repeated incursions by the barbarians of the north led him to leave. King Tai crossed mountain Liang after departing from Bin.
